title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text: Southern California has a lot of reasons for people to live there: Los Angeles is full of many areas to tour, though it also has a high crime rate. Meanwhile, Orange County is home to Disneyland, which is labeled as “the happiest place on earth”. Both counties also are home to beaches that attract tourists that have to travel and spend money doing so as opposed to people that live locally who can just drive to those beaches. My objective is to see if I can take any insight from house data in Southern California in the year 2025 to see if there is a difference between the prices in each county and do an inference on it.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Main Objective
The objective is to do some data wrangling to remove some prices that are clear outliers before doing analysis on the rest of the data. We are then going to make an inference about the relationship between price and county using Bayesian Statistics. We collected data on 7 variables: baths means number of bathrooms in the house while beds means the number of bedrooms in the house.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Design and Data Collection
The data was collected from somebody looking on Zillow for houses: it shows the city, price, beds, baths, area, type, and county that the data was collected in. This was collected at a specific date in 2025 (April 15), however, which very well could limit the analysis as it may not reflect things happening a month later when this project is finished. The variables also aren’t the best at giving insight as to why there may be a difference in prices between the cities because they only describe the house, not the other variables of the city.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Data Massaging
Something I noticed about the data was that SoCalRent2025 has commas and dashes in some of the observations of square feet. The variable sq ft is a character variable, so I had to make it numeric, but I had to change some things. First, I removed the commas from the numbers in the dataset to make them ready to be converted to a numeric variable.

SoCalRent2025 <- SoCalRent2025 %>% 
  mutate(
    `sq ft` = str_remove(`sq ft`, ",") #Remove commas in all numbers that have them
  )

That would make everything ready for converting square feet into a numerical variable, except that some of the entries in sq ft are what appear to be ranges with a “-” character. To do this, I ultimately decided to make two new variables: a minimum and a maximum variable for square feet so that both are represented to look at additional nuances of area.

SoCalRent2025 <- SoCalRent2025 %>% 
  mutate(
    min_sq_ft = if_else(str_detect(`sq ft`, "-"), 
    true = as.numeric(str_extract(`sq ft`, "[0-9]+")),
    false = as.numeric(`sq ft`),
    missing = NA), # Code to put the minimum square feet of the house, if there is a range of areas
    max_sq_ft = if_else(str_detect(`sq ft`, "-"),
    true = as.numeric(str_remove(str_extract(`sq ft`, "-[0-9]+$"), "-")),
    false = as.numeric(`sq ft`),
    missing = NA) # Code to put the maximum square feet of the house, if there is a range of areas
    )

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Let’s start with a general summary

SoCalRent2025 |>
  group_by(county) %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_price = mean(price),
    n = n() # Total number of houses by county
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  county mean_price     n
  <chr>       <dbl> <int>
1 LA          4313.   118
2 OC          4789.   110
3 RIV         2560.   100


This summary shows that the distribution is fairly even, with each county having 100 houses apiece. This was created ensure everything is almost equally represented. The dataset SoCalRent2025 features three counties: Los Angeles (LA), Orange (OC), and Riverside (RIV). The main thing that stood out was the mean price of LA County and Orange County are both much higher than that of Riverside, though I am mainly interested in focusing on LA County and Orange County to see if there was a difference between those two.

ggplot(SoCalRent2025, aes(x = price, y = county)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Price",
    y = "County"
  ) # Boxplots to see the relationship between price and county







 SoCalRent2025 %>%
   group_by(county) %>%
     summarize(
       min_price = min(price),
       q1_price = quantile(price, 0.25),
       med_price = median(price),
       q3_price = quantile(price, 0.75),
       max_price = max(price)
     ) # Numerical summary of the boxplot

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  county min_price q1_price med_price q3_price max_price
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 LA           750     2554     3500     4995      20000
2 OC          1500     2500     3908.    6150      30000
3 RIV          899     1920     2295     3196.      5000


This graph is displaying the amount of outliers that are present in the dataset in terms of price, and there are two are stick out like a sore thumb. Both are prices at or above $20000. The table is a numerical summary of the boxplots, which also shows the distribution of prices and shows how Orange County tends to have more expensive houses than the others, at least in this dataset. Both were created to show the distribution of prices by county.

SoCalRent2025 %>%
   filter(price >= 20000)

# A tibble: 2 × 9
  city       price  beds baths `sq ft` type  county min_sq_ft max_sq_ft
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>   <chr> <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>
1 west hills 20000     5     4 4180    house LA          4180      4180
2 anaheim    30000     2     2 2000    house OC          2000      2000


This figure shows the two outliers that I noticed. Right off the bat, a rent for $30000 in OC, a house in Anaheim that has 2 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms. It doesn’t sound like it is the norm, so we will remove this outlier. We can also filter out the $20000 rent in LA county because that is the other thing that is way above the rest of the prices, plus it’s a West Hills house that has the highest square feet, bedrooms, and bathrooms of all the remaining houses.

SoCalRent2025_1 <- SoCalRent2025 %>% 
  filter(price < 20000) # creating SoCalRent2025_1

ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = price, y = county)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Price",
    y = "County"
  )







SoCalRent2025_1 %>%
  group_by(county) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_price = mean(price)
  ) # numerical summary of the boxplot

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  county mean_price
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 LA          4179.
2 OC          4558.
3 RIV         2560.


These figures show the summaries after we have filtered out those data points. In the first figure, we bring it down to a maximum price of $14000 and a median price of $3097.5, which, considering how many houses over $10000 are in the dataset, make sense to keep, even if they’re considered outliers, since they’re close enough to the rest of the data. The second figure shows that Orange County, on average, has higher rent than Los Angeles County. One variable in the dataset that makes sense to explain this is square feet of the houses:

ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = min_sq_ft, y = county)) +
   geom_boxplot()

Warning: Removed 17 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).








ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = max_sq_ft, y = county)) +
   geom_boxplot()

Warning: Removed 19 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).









This histogram shows the square feet by county, adjusted by the minimum and maximum square feet for each house that had a range of areas. It was created to display the distribution of square feet by county as part of our exploratory data analysis.

ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = min_sq_ft, y = type)) +
   geom_boxplot() # using minimum square feet values

Warning: Removed 17 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).








ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = max_sq_ft, y = type)) +
   geom_boxplot() # using maximum square feet values

Warning: Removed 19 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).









This boxplot was created as a potential variable to explain square feet. We see from this graph that houses tend to be bigger than both condos and apartments. It is worth noting that apartments were the only things that had a range of values for their square feet, so not much changed between the condos and houses, but it is interesting that when we take the maximum square feet value for each apartment, they are very similar to condos.

SoCalRent2025_1 %>% 
  group_by(county, type) %>% 
  summarize(
    count = n()
  )

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'county'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.


# A tibble: 9 × 3
# Groups:   county [3]
  county type      count
  <chr>  <chr>     <int>
1 LA     apartment    38
2 LA     condo        40
3 LA     house        39
4 OC     apartment    32
5 OC     condo        39
6 OC     house        38
7 RIV    apartment    35
8 RIV    condo        25
9 RIV    house        40


Now we have to explore the distribution of house type by county, and it appears very even except for Riverside only having 25 condos. This ties into the counties all having similar average square feet in their houses, whether they were using the minimums or maximums.
Now, there are two different values due to some having ranges as part of their dataset. Here is a summary of the boxplots:

SoCalRent2025_1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(min_sq_ft)) |>
   group_by(county) %>% 
     summarize(
       minimum_sq_ft = min(min_sq_ft),
       q1_sq_ft = quantile(min_sq_ft, 0.25),
       med_sq_ft = median(min_sq_ft),
       q3_sq_ft = quantile(min_sq_ft, 0.75),
       max_sq_ft = max(min_sq_ft),
       mean_sq_ft = mean(min_sq_ft)
     ) # five-number summary with minimum square feet values

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  county minimum_sq_ft q1_sq_ft med_sq_ft q3_sq_ft max_sq_ft mean_sq_ft
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
1 LA               145      669      1102     1675      3000      1262.
2 OC               412      749      1153     1980      3339      1411.
3 RIV              355      750      1121     1576      3685      1239.


This first one is the square feet when taking all the minimum values for those in the range. We see there are places where they are very similar, such as the median, though the mean square feet of a residence in Orange County is relatively high compared to the mean square feet of the other two when using minimum values.

SoCalRent2025_1 %>%
  filter(!is.na(max_sq_ft)) %>% 
   group_by(county) %>%
     summarize(
       min_sq_ft = min(max_sq_ft),
       q1_sq_ft = quantile(max_sq_ft, 0.25),
       med_sq_ft = median(max_sq_ft),
       q3_sq_ft = quantile(max_sq_ft, 0.75),
       maximum_sq_ft = max(max_sq_ft),
       mean_sq_ft = mean(max_sq_ft)
     ) # five-number summary with maximum square feet values

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  county min_sq_ft q1_sq_ft med_sq_ft q3_sq_ft maximum_sq_ft mean_sq_ft
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 LA           145     1044      1318    1752.          3000      1440.
2 OC           446     1039      1310    2004.          3339      1534.
3 RIV          355      900      1152    1613           3685      1309.


So the datasets have quite some notable differences, though it may not be a fair representation as some of the minimum values by county don’t even change, labeling things as outliers when we look at all maximum prices even though they are not when we look at all the minimum prices. Square feet doesn’t appear to play a big factor, as they are all extremely similar between the counties.
And now, a histogram that shows the prices between the counties:

condition <- if_else(SoCalRent2025_1$price < 6000, "True", "False") # colors will be different depending on if price < 6000 or not on a histogram

ggplot(SoCalRent2025_1, aes(x = price, fill = condition)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  labs(
    title = "Rent Distrbution by County",
    x = "Price",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 24,
      face = "bold"
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 30, b = 30, l = 10),
    axis.title.x = element_text( # X-axis label
      size = 20
    ),
    axis.title.y = element_text( # X-axis label
      size = 20
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      size = 12
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(
      size = 16
    ),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(20, "points"),
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(county), ncol = 3, labeller = labeller(
               county = c(
                 "LA" = "Los Angeles County",
                 "OC" = "Orange County",
                 "RIV" = "Riverside County"
               )
             )) + # plots for each county
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("True" = "red", "False" = "blue"), labels = c(">=6000", "<6000")) # legend to show the condition








We can see that both Los Angeles County and Orange County have houses at or above $6000 in rent while none in Riverside have higher than about $5000. This definitely shows that Riverside houses tend to be cheaper to rent than those in Los Angeles County and Orange County. However, what I am mainly interested in is what the relationship between Los Angeles County and Orange County is like.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Modeling
In order to see the true relationship, let’s do some Bayesian Inference.

bayes_SoCalRent <- stan_glm(
  price ~ county,
  data = SoCalRent2025_1,
  family = "gaussian",
  prior = normal(location = 3, autoscale = TRUE),
  prior_intercept = default_prior_intercept(),
  seed = 1
)

Here, we are making a posterior distribution, which reflects updated beliefs after we have seen the housing rent data. This gives us an idea of what the relationship between the counties looks like.
The reference level is LA county, and we are comparing it to Orange County and Riverside County.

plot(
  bayes_SoCalRent,
  pars = c("countyOC", "countyRIV"),
  plotfun = "hist",
  bins = 15
) +
  labs(x = "Slope by county")








We can see from the graph that the rent in LA is clearly higher than in Riverside, but there doesn’t seem to be a significant difference between the rents of LA and Orange County.

predicted_house <- data.frame(
  county = c("OC", "RIV")
) # using the other two counties

predicted_rents <- bayes_SoCalRent %>% 
  posterior_predict(
    newdata = predicted_house,
    draws = 1000,
    seed = 1
  ) # make posterior predictions


predicted_rents_df <- predicted_rents %>% 
  as.data.frame()

ggplot(data = predicted_rents_df,
       mapping = aes(x = `1`)
       ) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20
  ) +
  labs(title = "Renting a House by county",
       x = "Rent Price",
       y = "Number of Simulated Houses"
  )








Predicted rent prices are pretty interesting, I experimented with a few priors, but all of them predicted negative rent price, so I just went with what I felt worked best.

bayes_SoCalRent |>
  posterior_interval(
      pars = c("countyOC", "countyRIV"),
      prob = 0.90
    )

                  5%        95%
countyOC   -100.7536   842.4131
countyRIV -2094.6339 -1135.4284


We can see that there is a 90% chance that the slope of the population model, assuming everything else stays constant, for an Orange County house compared to one in LA is between -100.7536 and 842.4131. This implies that there is no distinct difference in prices between the counties of LA and OC. There is also a 90% chance that the slope of the population model, assuming everything else stays constant, for a Riverside house compared to one in LA is between -2094.6339 and -1135.4284, meaning that Riverside houses tend to be cheaper to rent than LA houses.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Conclusion
Los Angeles County and Orange County are both great places to live in, and the rent of the houses in those places are very similar. There doesn’t appear to be a significant difference between the two counties. Riverside houses are much cheaper, but they also don’t offer the same things both Los Angeles County and Orange County do.

title: Comparing Rent Prices in SoCal Housing and Making Inferences
text:
Limitations
The data was collected on a specific date, so things may have changed by then. The problem is since they can change on a day-by-day basis, the data is not always the most accurate since houses can be taken off or rent could go up. Also, as mentioned earlier, there isn’t variables that are about the city, as the only one I could think of that was in the dataset with any real impact was square feet, and I didn’t feel like there was much of a difference between the counties’ average square feet.

title: Encelia Flower Model Selection
text:
Encelia californica is a plant in southern California that is pollinated frequently by bees. They are known as the California Bush Sunflower. Encelia farinosa, also known as desert brittle bush, is native to California deserts and frequently confused with Encelia californica. Encelia californica has yellow ray flowers and brown disk florets while Encelia farnosa has both yellow ray flowers and disk florets, with lighter-grayer green leaves than Encelia californica. California Bush Sunflowers also tend to be bigger than brittlebush in most areas. Both are found in the Fullerton Arboretum, where we went on a trip to get experience collecting data within our school. Through predictive modeling, we are trying to figure out what best predicts these flowers.
Being able to distinguish between these two species would be useful since one is an actual sunflower while one is just a bush. Both have slightly different uses: for example, a California Bush Sunflower is useful for controlling erosion while a brittlebush is useful for glue.

text:
Main Objective
The objective of this project is to be able to predict whether a flower is an Encelia californica or an Encelia farinosa using data that was gathered at the Fullerton Arboretum. Through four variables and a brief description of the differences between the flowers, we have an idea of what models we select. We are performing model selection in order to determine what is the best predictor of flowers.

title: Encelia Flower Model Selection
text:
Design and Data Collection
The data was collected from the Fullerton Arboretum by our class. We had 5 different pairs survey 20 different flowers each. We decided to track four variables: The number of rays/petals of the flower; the disk diameter, which is the diameter of the inside of the flower; the ray diameter, which is the diameter of a ray/petal in the flower, and the stem length, which was measured from the bottom to the top of the flower. Species is labeled as ‘F’ for Encelia farinosa or ‘C’ for Encelia californica.
One group forgot to measure stem length of the flowers that they sampled, which explains why some of the data values were NA. Additionally, it is very possible that some of these flowers are the exact same because different groups may have went to the exact same flower or a flower was surveyed twice. It is also possible that these are not exact measurements, and there may be different data for the same class. We have decided to round each numerical value that is continuous to the nearest tenth, whereas some other person may round to two decimal points. Also, we may have different definitions of the variables, such as stem length being only to nearest branch. We may also have different variables entirely from what another person chose, but we chose 4 variables, all numerical, whereas somebody may use a categorical variable such as the color of the disk floret. We did try to get flowers in various locations, as location can also affect characteristics of a flower.

title: Encelia Flower Model Selection
text:
Training-Test Split

encelia_data <- readr::read_csv(here::here("../Data", "Encelia Classification Data Collection - Sheet1.csv"))

Rows: 100 Columns: 5

Delimiter: ","

ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

encelia_data <- encelia_data %>% # spell out flower names
  mutate(
    Species = if_else(Species == "F", "Encelia Farinosa", "Encelia Californica") %>% 
      as.factor()
  )

I ultimately decided to spell out the names of the flowers for exploratory data analysis purposes when we see the graphs later.

set.seed(3)
encelia_split <- initial_split(
  encelia_data,
  strata = Species,
  prop = 0.80
) # 80% of flowers will go to the training set, and roughly the same proportion of species will go in each set
  
encelia_train <- training(encelia_split)
encelia_test <- testing(encelia_split)

Training and test sets are necessary because we are training a model on the training set, doing explanatory data analysis and modeling on the training set. We are then using the test set to validate our predictions and models to see how accurate it is. By doing this, we are using the encelia training set to do some exploration and model fitting before testing the models on the testing set to see how well they predict the species of the flower.

title: Encelia Flower Model Selection
text:
Modeling
So, after looking at the graphs and summaries above, these are the following models I came up with that I feel like are really good predictors based on my explanatory data analysis:

Number of Rays
Stem Length
Stem Length + Number of Rays
Ray Diameter + Number of Rays
Ray Diameter + Disk Diameter
Stem Length + Ray Diameter
Ray Diameter

I also believe that doing a combination of Number of Rays, Ray Diameter, and Stem Length would also be a decent model to explore as the flowers. They have big differences in number of rays and stem length, and some variation in ray diameter, so I think combining these three would make for a great prediction. As I said in the context, Encelia Californica tend to be bigger than Encelia Farinosa, and those three attributes are what they tend to be bigger in.

contrasts(encelia_train$Species)

                    Encelia Farinosa
Encelia Californica                0
Encelia Farinosa                   1


Anyways, with the potential predictors being identified, we will perform logistic regression. Logistic regression is the probability that an observation is categorized as something. In this case, we are looking at the probability a flower is an Encelia Farinosa vs an Encelia Californica based on characteristics. This is done so that we see how well models can predict the species of the flowers and how effectively it can tell the difference between the two.
We start off by making some folds. These give us non-overlapping subsets of the training set that, with the exception of one, we will be testing our model on.

set.seed(3)
encelia_cv <- encelia_train %>% 
  vfold_cv(
    v = 5, # 5-fold cv
    repeats = 1 # one unique prediction per observation in training set
  )

After we have made the folds, we will now use the models that I believe are good predictors of the plant species.

encelia_predictions <- function(split){
  # this function takes in cross-validated splits
  
  train <- analysis(split)
  valid <- assessment(split)
  
  glm_null <- glm(Species ~ 1, data = train, family = "binomial") # the null model is there, as always, to see which, if any, of those possible predictors are worse than the null model
  glm1 <- glm(Species ~ number_rays, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm2 <- glm(Species ~ stem_length, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm3 <- glm(Species ~ stem_length + number_rays, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm4 <- glm(Species ~ ray_diameter + number_rays, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm5 <- glm(Species ~ disk_diameter + ray_diameter, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm6 <- glm(Species ~ stem_length + ray_diameter, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm7 <- glm(Species ~ ray_diameter, data = train, family = "binomial")
  glm8 <- glm(Species ~ number_rays + stem_length + ray_diameter, data = train, family = "binomial")
  
  valid_predictions <- valid %>% 
    mutate(
      pred_null = predict(glm_null, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_num_rays = predict(glm1, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_stem_len = predict(glm2, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_stem_len_num_rays = predict(glm3, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_ray_dia_num_rays = predict(glm4, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_disk_dia_ray_dia = predict(glm5, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_stem_len_ray_dia = predict(glm6, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_ray_dia = predict(glm7, newdata = valid, type = "response"),
      pred_3 = predict(glm8, newdata = valid, type = "response")
    )
  
  return(valid_predictions)
}


mapped_predictions <- map(
  encelia_cv$splits, # list to input to function
  encelia_predictions # function to apply
)

We then fit the best model onto the test set. The model I selected was the model that predicts species based on stem length and number of rays. Not only did it have the lowest Brier Score, with the next closest one adding ray diameter to these two variables, but they also had the most notable differences between the species.
Now that we have fit the final models on the test set, we will compute the confusion matrix to see how accurate the model is:

encelia_class_predictions %>% 
  conf_mat(
    truth = Species,
    estimate = .pred_class
  )

                     Truth
Prediction            Encelia Californica Encelia Farinosa
  Encelia Californica                   7                1
  Encelia Farinosa                      1                8


Based on this confusion matrix, it is extremely accurate! In this test set, it only predicted two flowers wrong, one of each species. In total, it predicted 7 of 8 Encelia Californica flowers correctly and 8 of 9 Encelia Farinosa flowers correctly, and it overall predicted 15 of the 17 flowers correctly.

text:
Insights

roc_df <- encelia_class_predictions %>% 
  roc_curve(
    truth = Species,
    .fitted,
    event_level = "second"
  )

autoplot(roc_df)







encelia_class_predictions %>% 
  roc_auc(
    truth = Species,
    .fitted,
    event_level = "second"
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 roc_auc binary         0.861


This receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve shows the true positive and false positive rates for Encelia Farinosa. We see that everything is above the dotted line, which means that the model selected outputs a good prediction at all thresholds. The area under the curve is 0.8611111, which isn’t perfect, but it is better than a coin flip chance at predicting Encelia Farinosa correctly at each decision threshold. Considering that Encelia Californica is bigger than an Encelia Farinosa,

encelia_class_predictions %>% 
  filter(Species != .pred_class)

# A tibble: 2 × 9
  Species     number_rays disk_diameter ray_diameter stem_length .fitted .pred_F
  <fct>             <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Encelia Ca…          11           1            3.3           3   0.997   0.997
2 Encelia Fa…          11           1.5          3            23   0.144   0.144
# ℹ 2 more variables: .pred_C <dbl>, .pred_class <fct>


For these two flowers that were incorrectly predicted, both have the same number of rays. However, something jumps out: the species that was an Encelia Farinosa was predicted an Encelia Californica because of its stem length of 23 cm, in which a large stem length is typical of Encelia Californica. On the other side, an Encelia Californica was predicted as an Encelia Farinosa has a stem length of 3 cm and Encelia Farinosa have shorter stem lengths than Encelia Californica on average. I believe these are outliers and that they were either misclassified or are an oddity in a group of flowers that were predcited correctly otherwise.
